questions.question: How do you configure Caffeine cache properly in Spring Boot — sizing, eviction, refresh, stats?
questions.title: Caffeine Cache: Configuration, Policies, Stats
questions.direct_answer: Caffeine is the default in-process Java cache: it replaces Guava Cache, uses the Window TinyLFU admission policy (near-optimal hit rate), and integrates cleanly with Spring's `@Cacheable`. Production config needs four things: **(1) bound size** with `maximumSize` or `maximumWeight` — never unbounded; **(2) expiry** with `expireAfterWrite` or `expireAfterAccess` depending on freshness vs hit-rate priority; **(3) `refreshAfterWrite`** for async background refresh on hot keys; **(4) `recordStats()`** + Micrometer binding to monitor hit rate, eviction, load latency. Also set `softValues()` or heap weighting cautiously; prefer bounded eviction over GC pressure. Request coalescing (`CacheLoader`) prevents thundering herd for free.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Unbounded cache; no stats; expireAfterAccess when expireAfterWrite fits; missing request coalescing; ignoring heap pressure
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Window TinyLFU, async refresh, weigher for variable-size entries, Caffeine + Spring Cache integration, metric export

sections.title: Why Caffeine Over Guava and ConcurrentHashMap
sections.content:
Caffeine is the modern Java in-process cache. Written by Ben Manes (formerly Guava Cache), it's the successor Google recommends — faster, better hit rate, richer features. If you're using Guava Cache in 2026, migrate.

**What Caffeine adds over `ConcurrentHashMap`:**
- **Size-bound eviction** with Window TinyLFU (near-optimal hit rate; much better than LRU)
- **Time-based expiry** (`expireAfterWrite`, `expireAfterAccess`, `expireAfter` custom)
- **Async loading & refresh** (background refresh without blocking reads)
- **Request coalescing** via `CacheLoader` (thundering herd free)
- **Statistics** (`recordStats()`) for observability
- **Weighted capacity** (different entries count differently)
- **Weak / soft references** for GC-friendly caching
- **Write-through** and **write-behind** options

**Window TinyLFU** is the killer feature. LRU evicts the least-recently-used; in workloads with scans or one-hit-wonders, LRU thrashes. TinyLFU uses frequency sketches (count-min sketch) to admit only items likely to be re-accessed, protecting hot data. Near-optimal in most real workloads.

Caffeine is the default Spring Cache provider when `spring-boot-starter-cache` + `caffeine` are on the classpath.

sections.title: Spring Boot Configuration
Eviction Policies and Sizing
sections.content:
**Size limits:**
- `maximumSize(N)` — entry count (simplest)
- `maximumWeight(N)` + `weigher((k,v) -> ...)` — when entries vary significantly in size (HTML fragments, serialized objects)

**Expiry:**
- `expireAfterWrite(d)` — entry expires d after write (freshness priority)
- `expireAfterAccess(d)` — entry expires d after last access (hit-rate priority)
- `expireAfter(Expiry)` — per-entry custom TTL (e.g., longer TTL for popular products)

**Refresh:**
- `refreshAfterWrite(d)` — async reload after d; old value served until reload
- Stricter than `expireAfterWrite` — keep data flowing without user-visible misses

**Reference types:**
- `weakKeys()` / `weakValues()` — eligible for GC when no strong reference elsewhere
- `softValues()` — evicted under memory pressure
- Use sparingly — most production uses bounded sizes instead

**Typical configurations by use case:**

| Use Case | maximumSize | expireAfterWrite | refreshAfterWrite |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature flags | 1,000 | 5 min | 1 min |
| User profiles | 10,000 | 15 min | 5 min |
| Product pages | 50,000 | 30 min | 10 min |
| Hot config | 500 | 10 min | 2 min |
| Computation results | 10,000 | 1 hour | — |
| Session data | 50,000 | 30 min (access) | — |

**Sizing heuristics:**
- Size × avg entry bytes must fit comfortably in heap (leave 30–50% headroom)
- Start at 10k entries; tune based on hit rate metrics
- Monitor eviction rate; if very high, cache too small
- Monitor hit rate; if very low, cache not useful or TTL too short

**Heap pressure warning.**
Unbounded cache or too-large `maximumSize` can cause long GC pauses. Always bound. For large objects, prefer `maximumWeight` + `weigher`. Heap monitoring (JVM GC logs, Prometheus heap metrics) is mandatory.

sections.title: Observability and Metrics
Trade-offs and Gotchas
sections.content:
**Per-instance state.** Caffeine cache is per-JVM. In a 10-instance cluster, same key loads 10 times and 10 independent copies exist. Don't use for counters, quotas, or anything requiring cluster-wide truth — those need Redis.

**Invalidation across instances.** When one instance updates the DB, other instances' Caffeine caches are stale. Solutions:
- Short TTL (accept stale for TTL window)
- Redis pub/sub invalidation message
- Event-driven invalidation (Kafka event when data changes)
- CDC (Debezium) → invalidation events

**GC impact.** Every Caffeine entry is a Java object holding references. 100k entries with 10KB each = ~1GB heap. Set bounds conservatively; monitor GC pause times.

**`expireAfterAccess` can keep garbage hot.** If only scanned by background process, items stay 'accessed'. Usually `expireAfterWrite` is safer default.

**`sync = true` on `@Cacheable` is often forgotten.** Without it, concurrent cache-miss requests all call the underlying loader (thundering herd). With `sync = true`, Caffeine coalesces.

**`@CacheEvict(allEntries = true)` is expensive** and usually wrong. Clears entire cache; subsequent requests all miss. Prefer per-key eviction.

**Key serialization.** Caffeine uses Java `.equals()`/`.hashCode()` on keys. Mutable keys break caching. Use immutable key objects (records, Strings, Longs).

**Spring Cache abstraction limits.** `@Cacheable` only supports the lowest common denominator; Caffeine-specific features (async loading, refresh) need direct Caffeine usage. For complex cases, inject `Cache<K,V>` directly.

**Spring Cache `null` values.** By default, Spring caches `null` as `NullValue.INSTANCE`. If you don't want to cache nulls: `@Cacheable(unless = "#result == null")`.

**Caffeine is not for big entries.** 10MB entries belong on disk or in Redis — not in heap. Caffeine shines for millions of small entries.

**Caffeine vs EhCache.** EhCache was dominant pre-2020; Caffeine is faster and simpler. EhCache 3 with Terracotta adds distribution but is rarely chosen over Redis in new systems.

**Caffeine vs ConcurrentHashMap + scheduled cleanup.** You can build cache in CHM, but you'll reinvent TinyLFU, stats, expiry, async loading — poorly. Just use Caffeine.

**Warm-up strategy.** Fresh JVM = empty cache. First minutes may hit DB hard. Options:
- Warm cache at startup for hot keys (`@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent)`)
- Gradual rollout (canary) with LB slow ramp
- Replica 'reading' from old instance before cutover

**Tiered caching.** Caffeine (L1) + Redis (L2) gives best of both. Pattern:
1. Check Caffeine
2. On miss, check Redis
3. On miss, load from DB
4. Populate both on the way up
5. Publish invalidation event on writes

**Single flight / request coalescing.** Caffeine's `LoadingCache` does this automatically — concurrent gets for the same absent key share one load. Hugely valuable.

**Don't cache responses with security implications thoughtlessly.** A `@Cacheable` method returning user's data keyed by request params without tenant/user in the key = cross-tenant leak. Always include user/tenant in key or namespace the cache.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Caffeine is the 2026 default in-process cache** in Java; replaces Guava
- **Window TinyLFU admission** gives near-optimal hit rate vs LRU
- **Always bound**: `maximumSize` or `maximumWeight` + `weigher`
- **Expiry options**: `expireAfterWrite` (freshness) vs `expireAfterAccess` (hit rate) vs `expireAfter` (custom)
- **`refreshAfterWrite` for async refresh** on hot keys; users never see misses
- **Request coalescing** (sync=true / LoadingCache) prevents thundering herd free
- **`recordStats()` + Micrometer** for hit rate, eviction, load latency dashboards
- **Per-instance only** — use Redis for cluster-wide state or invalidate via pub/sub
- **Include tenant/user in key** to avoid cross-tenant leaks
- **Spring `@Cacheable` with `sync=true`** is essential for hot keys

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Caffeine is the default in-process Java cache in 2026. It replaces Guava Cache (same author, Ben Manes) and uses Window TinyLFU admission policy for near-optimal hit rate.

**What Caffeine adds over ConcurrentHashMap**
- Size-bound eviction with Window TinyLFU
- Time-based expiry (expireAfterWrite, expireAfterAccess)
- Async loading and refresh
- Request coalescing (thundering herd free)
- Statistics for observability
- Weighted capacity for variable-size entries

**Why Window TinyLFU over LRU**
- LRU evicts least-recently-used; in workloads with scans or one-hit-wonders, LRU thrashes
- TinyLFU uses frequency sketches; admits only items likely to be re-accessed
- Protects hot data; near-optimal in most real workloads

**Spring Boot configuration**
- Dependencies: spring-boot-starter-cache + caffeine
- @EnableCaching plus CaffeineCacheManager with global Caffeine builder
- Or per-cache config with SimpleCacheManager for different sizes and TTLs

**Production config needs four things**

*(1) Bound size*
- maximumSize(N) by entry count
- maximumWeight(N) + weigher for variable-size entries
- Never unbounded

*(2) Expiry*
- expireAfterWrite: entry expires after d from write; freshness priority
- expireAfterAccess: expires after d from last access; hit-rate priority
- expireAfter(Expiry): per-entry custom TTL
- expireAfterWrite is the safer default; expireAfterAccess can keep garbage hot

*(3) refreshAfterWrite for async background refresh*
- After d, next read triggers async reload
- Old value served until reload completes
- Users never see misses on hot keys
- Stricter than expireAfterWrite

*(4) recordStats() plus Micrometer binding*
- Hit rate, eviction, load latency
- CaffeineCacheMetrics.monitor() for each cache
- Grafana alerts: hit ratio below 80%, eviction spike, load duration high

**Usage with Spring @Cacheable**
- @Cacheable(value = products, key = #id, sync = true)
- sync = true is critical: prevents thundering herd; coalesces concurrent requests
- @CacheEvict per key; avoid allEntries=true

**Async patterns**
- LoadingCache with refreshAfterWrite for hot data
- AsyncLoadingCache returning CompletableFuture for I/O loaders

**Typical configurations**
- Feature flags: 1k entries, 5 min TTL, 1 min refresh
- User profiles: 10k entries, 15 min TTL, 5 min refresh
- Product pages: 50k entries, 30 min TTL, 10 min refresh
- Session data: 50k entries, 30 min access-based

**Sizing heuristics**
- Size times avg entry bytes must fit comfortably in heap (30 to 50% headroom)
- Start at 10k entries; tune via hit rate metrics
- High eviction rate means cache too small
- Low hit rate means cache not useful or TTL too short

**Observability — key metrics**
- cache.size
- cache.gets (hit + miss)
- cache.evictions
- cache.hit.ratio
- cache.load.duration
- cache.load.failure

**Trade-offs and gotchas**

*Per-instance state*
- Caffeine is per-JVM
- 10-instance cluster means 10 independent copies
- Don't use for counters, quotas, cluster-wide truth — use Redis

*Invalidation across instances*
- Short TTL (accept stale)
- Redis pub/sub invalidation
- Event-driven invalidation (Kafka)
- CDC to invalidation events

*GC impact*
- Every entry is a Java object
- 100k entries of 10KB each equals about 1GB heap
- Bound conservatively; monitor GC pauses

*Thundering herd without sync=true*
- Concurrent cache-miss requests all call loader
- Always use sync=true for hot keys
- LoadingCache coalesces automatically

*@CacheEvict(allEntries=true)*
- Expensive; clears entire cache
- Prefer per-key eviction

*Mutable keys break caching*
- Use immutable key objects (records, Strings, Longs)

*Big entries don't belong here*
- 10MB entries go on disk or Redis
- Caffeine shines for millions of small entries

*Cross-tenant cache leaks*
- A @Cacheable method keyed by request params without tenant ID means cross-tenant leak
- Always include user or tenant in key or namespace the cache

**Tiered caching — Caffeine L1 plus Redis L2**
- Check Caffeine; on miss check Redis; on miss load DB
- Populate both on way up
- Publish invalidation event on writes
- Best of both worlds

**Warm-up strategy**
- Fresh JVM means empty cache; first minutes hit DB hard
- Warm at startup with @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent)
- Gradual rollout (canary) with LB slow ramp

**Caffeine vs alternatives**
- vs Guava Cache: Caffeine is faster, better hit rate, actively maintained
- vs EhCache: Caffeine simpler and faster; EhCache with Terracotta rarely chosen over Redis
- vs ConcurrentHashMap: just use Caffeine

**The strategic answer**
- Default in-process Java cache; superseded Guava
- Always bound; prefer expireAfterWrite; add refreshAfterWrite for hot data
- Enable recordStats and Micrometer binding
- Use sync=true to avoid thundering herd
- Per-instance only; use Redis for cluster-wide
- Combine as L1 with Redis L2 for high-traffic apps
- Watch heap pressure and GC

steps: Dependencies: ``xml <dependency> <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId> <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-cache</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId> <artifactId>caffeine</artifactId> </dependency> ` Enable caching + programmatic Caffeine config (recommended over application.yml for fine control): `java @Configuration @EnableCaching public class CacheConfig { @Bean public CacheManager cacheManager() { CaffeineCacheManager mgr = new CaffeineCacheManager( "products", "userProfiles", "featureFlags"); mgr.setCaffeine(Caffeine.newBuilder() .maximumSize(10_000) .expireAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(10)) .refreshAfterWrite(Duration.ofMinutes(2)) .recordStats()); return mgr; } } ` Per-cache custom config (different sizes/TTLs per cache): `java @Bean public CacheManager cacheManager() { SimpleCacheManager mgr = new SimpleCacheManager(); mgr.setCaches(List.of( caffeineCache("products", 50_000, Duration.ofMinutes(30)), caffeineCache("featureFlags", 1_000, Duration.ofMinutes(5)), caffeineCache("userProfiles", 10_000, Duration.ofMinutes(15)) )); return mgr; } private CaffeineCache caffeineCache(String name, long size, Duration ttl) { return new CaffeineCache(name, Caffeine.newBuilder() .maximumSize(size) .expireAfterWrite(ttl) .recordStats() .build()); } ` Usage with @Cacheable: `java @Service public class ProductService { @Cacheable(value = "products", key = "#id", sync = true) public Product findById(String id) { return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); } @CacheEvict(value = "products", key = "#p.id") public void update(Product p).
